title: Questions before SYT2 and SNAP25 groups join forces

sentences.text: Given the disputed link between SNAP25 and reduced protein function, which patients share this problem with SYT2 patients, and which have a protein that does too much?
How strong is the evidence that one working gene copy is not enough in either condition, given that these links are inferred rather than directly tested?
How strong is the evidence that SYT2 helps calcium trigger the release of nerve messages?
How strong is the evidence that SNAP25 helps packets carrying nerve messages join the nerve cell membrane to release their contents?
Do the different inheritance patterns in SYT2 and SNAP25 change who can join a shared study?
Do the eligibility rules and visit schedule of the amifampridine phosphate study suit both groups equally, given its requirement for genetically confirmed congenital myasthenic syndromes?
Given the different mixes of gene changes in SYT2 and SNAP25, would ways of measuring progress developed for one group work for the other?
Are increased muscle electrical responses during repeated nerve stimulation and limited eye movements truly absent in SNAP25, or simply not documented?
What would Simons Searchlight need to change to include SYT2 families alongside SNAP25 families?
Could the Congenital Muscle Disease International Registry or RARE-X support shared data collection for both communities?
